questions.stem: Methane reacts with bromine under ultraviolet light to give bromomethane and hydrogen bromide. Which type of reaction is this?

options.text: Substitution, because a hydrogen atom is replaced by bromine
options.explanation: One atom in the methane is swapped for another, which is the defining move of a substitution reaction.

options.text: Addition, because the molecules combine
options.explanation: Two products form here; addition would leave one merged product and nothing else.

options.text: Combustion, because bromine is reactive
options.explanation: Combustion means burning in oxygen; no oxygen takes part in this reaction.

options.text: No classification applies without a mechanism
options.explanation: Mechanisms are not required; the type follows from what the equation shows.

questions.stem: What is the defining feature of an addition reaction?

options.text: Two or more molecules form one larger molecule with no other products
options.explanation: Everything that enters the reaction leaves inside the single merged product.

options.text: One atom swaps places with another inside the molecule
options.explanation: That describes substitution, which produces two products rather than one.

options.text: The molecule burns in a plentiful oxygen supply
options.explanation: Burning in oxygen is combustion, the third type, not addition.

options.text: A catalyst is always required for the reaction to proceed
options.explanation: Addition needs no catalyst in general; the definition is about merging molecules.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with bromine to give C2H4Br2. Why is this an addition reaction?

options.text: Both bromine atoms add across the double bond, leaving one product
options.explanation: The two reactant molecules merge into dibromoethane alone, which is the addition signature.

options.text: Because ethene is an alkane with strong bonds
options.explanation: Ethene is an alkene, and the classification rests on the single merged product.

options.text: Because a hydrogen atom was replaced by bromine
options.explanation: No hydrogen leaves the molecule here; the bromine joins on across the double bond.

options.text: Because the reaction needs ultraviolet light to start
options.explanation: Ultraviolet light belongs to the alkane-halogen substitution story, not this addition.

questions.stem: How many products does a substitution reaction produce from one organic molecule and one attacking molecule?

options.text: Two products: the substituted molecule and the displaced fragment
options.explanation: What leaves the organic molecule pairs with the incoming atom to form the second product, as in HBr.

options.text: One product only, because everything merges
options.explanation: One merged product describes addition; substitution always has something displaced.

options.text: Three products in every case
options.explanation: The standard substitution makes exactly two products at this level.

options.text: It depends on the temperature used
options.explanation: The product count follows from the reaction type, not the temperature.

questions.stem: Do you need to know reaction mechanisms for this classification work?

options.text: No, classifying as substitution, addition or combustion is enough
options.explanation: The specification explicitly excludes mechanisms; naming the type is the required skill.

options.text: Yes, every classification needs the full mechanism quoted
options.explanation: Mechanisms are beyond the requirement; the type label alone is the marking point.

options.text: Only for addition reactions
options.explanation: No reaction type at this level demands a mechanism for classification.

options.text: Only when the reaction happens in sunlight
options.explanation: Light conditions help identify substitution, but mechanisms stay excluded everywhere.

questions.stem: What are the products when methane burns completely in air?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.explanation: Unlimited oxygen oxidises every carbon fully to CO2, with hydrogen ending as water.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide belongs to incomplete burning in a limited oxygen supply.

options.text: Carbon and hydrogen only
options.explanation: With oxygen present the products are oxides, not the bare elements.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas
options.explanation: Hydrogen from the fuel joins oxygen to make water, not hydrogen gas.

questions.stem: Which condition produces carbon monoxide during the burning of a hydrocarbon?

options.text: A limited supply of air or oxygen
options.explanation: Starved of oxygen, the carbon cannot fully oxidise and settles for monoxide.

options.text: An unlimited supply of oxygen
options.explanation: Plentiful oxygen drives complete burning to carbon dioxide instead.

options.text: The presence of nitrogen in the air
options.explanation: Nitrogen is already in air during complete burning too; only the oxygen shortage matters.

options.text: Any temperature below 100 degrees Celsius
options.explanation: Temperature alone does not decide the products; the oxygen supply does.

questions.stem: Balance the complete equation: CH4 + ? O2 -> CO2 + ? H2O

options.text: 2 before O2 and 2 before H2O
options.explanation: Four hydrogens need two waters, and those two waters plus CO2 need four oxygens, so 2O2 supplies them.

options.text: 1 before O2 and 2 before H2O
options.explanation: One O2 gives only two oxygens, but CO2 and 2H2O together need four.

options.text: 2 before O2 and 1 before H2O
options.explanation: One water leaves two hydrogens stranded from the four that methane carries.

options.text: 4 before O2 and 4 before H2O
options.explanation: That over-supplies oxygen and breaks the atom balance the equation must keep.

questions.stem: In an oxygen-poor appliance, what can form from methane instead of carbon dioxide?

options.text: Carbon monoxide, or carbon soot in very poor supply
options.explanation: The note shows both routes: 2CH4 + 3O2 to CO, and CH4 + O2 all the way down to carbon.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide, from the methane itself
options.explanation: Methane carries no sulfur; SO2 arises from impurities in other fuels.

options.text: Nothing, because methane cannot burn without full oxygen
options.explanation: Incomplete burning is still burning; it simply stops at CO or carbon.

options.text: Only water, with the carbon vanishing
options.explanation: Atoms are conserved; the carbon must appear as CO, soot or CO2, never vanish.

questions.stem: Why is combustion classified alongside substitution and addition?

options.text: Because it is one of the three named types of organic reaction
options.explanation: The classification scheme of the topic lists exactly these three reaction families.

options.text: Because it only happens to alkanes
options.explanation: The note records alkenes burning too, so the type is not alkane-only.

options.text: Because it needs ultraviolet light like substitution
options.explanation: Combustion needs oxygen and a flame or spark, not ultraviolet radiation.

options.text: Because it produces one merged product
options.explanation: Two products, CO2 and water, form in complete burning, so it is not an addition case.
